# Fill-rule simulation — does 40-at-12h seal often enough?

**Generated by `scripts/sim/fill-replay.ts`. Do not edit by hand — re-run it.**

It answers one question: on realistic arrival curves, how often does the 40-at-12h rule seal a pool rather than refund it?

## What it says

**Read this first.** The simulated arrivals follow an assumed country mix (below), and under territory schedule version 5 **49% of that mix is blocked** at the entry gate. The figures therefore depend heavily on that assumption; the "Mean seated" column is what actually reaches a seat.

**Floor 40 against floor 52.** Averaged over 40-55 attempts in 12 hours, the 40-seat floor refunds **99%** of pools; the old 52-seat floor refunded **100%** on the same arrivals. The full curve is in the table below.

**The rate you need.** A pool refunds less than one time in ten once attempts reach about **100 in 12 hours** — roughly 8.3 an hour, sustained. Below that, refunds are common; the rule is working, the audience is not there yet.

**What a pool returns.** A pool sealing at the floor returns nothing — by design, because the prize pool equals forty entries (decision R7-b). The "mean return" column is the average over pools that ran, and it stays well under the 2.4 SOL of a full field until arrivals are comfortably above capacity, because a pool that seals at the deadline usually seals near the floor rather than near 64.

## What was simulated

- Floor **40** seats (R7-b), capacity **64**, window **12 hours**.
- Tier 0: entry 0.100 SOL, prize pool 4.000 SOL.
- 2,000 pools per arrival rate, Poisson arrivals, one seeded PRNG.
- Territory schedule version 5 (block-list), blocking: AE, AU, BE, BH, CN, ES, FR, HK, ID, IN, IT, KW, MY, OM, QA, SA, SG, US.

## The result

| Mean arrivals in 12h | Seals at 64 | Seals at deadline | **Refunds** | Refunds at the old 52-seat floor | Mean seated | Blocked by territory | Mean return per pool that ran |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 | 0.0% | 0.0% | **100.0%** | 100.0% | 15.3 | 14.7 | 0.000 SOL |
| 40 | 0.0% | 0.0% | **100.0%** | 100.0% | 20.3 | 19.7 | 0.000 SOL |
| 45 | 0.0% | 0.1% | **100.0%** | 100.0% | 23.0 | 22.0 | 0.000 SOL |
| 50 | 0.0% | 0.7% | **99.3%** | 100.0% | 25.4 | 24.4 | 0.107 SOL |
| 55 | 0.0% | 2.4% | **97.6%** | 100.0% | 28.1 | 26.9 | 0.143 SOL |
| 64 | 0.0% | 10.2% | **89.8%** | 100.0% | 32.5 | 31.2 | 0.232 SOL |
| 80 | 0.1% | 58.0% | **41.9%** | 94.8% | 40.9 | 39.1 | 0.523 SOL |
| 100 | 4.2% | 90.8% | **5.0%** | 55.0% | 50.8 | 49.2 | 1.151 SOL |

Note the arrival rate is **attempts**, before the territory gate — the "mean seated"
column is what actually reaches a seat, and the gap between them is the blocked share.

## The adversarial case

One seat short of the floor until the last minute, and the seat that would have saved it arrives one second after the deadline.

- Outcome: **refunded**, 39 seated, 39 refunded.
- Rejected by the deadline: 1.
- Under the old 52-seat floor the same timeline: **refunded**.

This is the case worth being uncomfortable about: it refunds, and it refunds for the
sake of one second. It is also the case the rule is supposed to produce — the
alternative is a clock that moves, and a clock that moves is a clock the operator
chooses. Nothing here is a bug; it is the cost of the boundary being strict.

## What this does not model

- **Demand is exogenous.** A pool that refunds probably depresses the next one, and a
  pool that fills fast probably raises it. There is no feedback term, so these are
  first-order estimates, not a forecast.
- **Arrivals are independent.** Real entries cluster around whatever is posted, and
  clustering RAISES the seal rate at a given mean by making the count less random.
  The refund percentages above are therefore pessimistic.
- **The country mix is a guess**, labelled as one. It exercises the territory gate;
  it is not a claim about where demand will be.
- **Sanctions screening is not simulated** — it rejects by wallet against live lists,
  which a country code cannot stand in for.
